title: 10 Jul 2025
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall, 10 July 2025. Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A child has fever for 7 days, conjunctival injection and cervical lymphadenopathy, and is treated for Kawasaki disease. Which complication is the treatment meant to prevent?
questions.exp: IVIG (with aspirin) given within 10 days of fever onset lowers the risk of coronary artery aneurysms from about 25% to under 5%. Aneurysms can cause thrombosis, stenosis, myocardial infarction and sudden death.

questions.question: A child with Kawasaki disease has fever, a high ESR and thrombocytosis. What is the management?
questions.b: IVIG and aspirin, with an echocardiogram
questions.exp: Treat with IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, and do an echocardiogram at diagnosis and at 2 and 6 weeks. Thrombocytosis typically appears in the second week; it is part of the disease, not a reason to delay treatment.

questions.question: A 5-year-old's fever subsided and then a rash appeared on the trunk. He looks well. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Roseola (HHV-6): high fever for several days, then a pink macular rash on the trunk as the fever falls, in a well child. It usually affects children under 3 years, but older children can be affected.

questions.question: A child had fever and a rash after coryzal symptoms (measles). Which complication can occur years later?
questions.exp: SSPE is a fatal, progressive encephalitis 7–10 years after measles (risk higher when infected under 2 years), with myoclonus, cognitive decline and periodic EEG complexes. Vaccination prevents it.

questions.question: A teenager has fever, sore throat and fatigue. The blood film shows atypical lymphocytes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: EBV infectious mononucleosis: fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical (reactive) lymphocytes. Confirm with Monospot or EBV serology; avoid contact sport for 3–4 weeks.

questions.question: A child is ill with fever and a non-blanching rash. Blood culture grows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci. Which statement is true?
questions.e: Antibiotics for contacts are not needed
questions.exp: Meningococcal disease: give IV ceftriaxone urgently, fluid resuscitation for shock, and chemoprophylaxis to close contacts. MenB and MenACWY conjugate vaccines prevent it.

questions.question: A child from Bangladesh has bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Which organism is the likely cause?
questions.exp: Amoebic dysentery: bloody, mucoid stools with tenesmus and abdominal pain, sometimes liver abscess. Treat with metronidazole then a luminal agent. Shigella and Campylobacter are the main bacterial causes of dysentery.

questions.question: A child with tympanostomy (grommet) tubes has ear discharge with no fever. What is the treatment?
questions.a: Topical antibiotic ear drops such as ciprofloxacin
questions.exp: Acute otorrhoea through a grommet is treated with topical quinolone drops (ciprofloxacin, ± steroid), which are effective and not ototoxic, plus aural toilet. Oral antibiotics are for systemic illness or failed topical treatment. Avoid aminoglycoside drops.

questions.question: Four hours after an appendicectomy for a ruptured appendix, a child has fever of 39°C, capillary refill of 3–4 seconds and low blood pressure. What is the first step?
questions.b: Return to theatre before any fluid
questions.d: A 0.9% saline bolus (10–20 mL/kg) with broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.e: Start an adrenaline infusion before fluid
questions.exp: This is septic shock (peritonitis). Give oxygen, IV/IO access, fluid boluses with reassessment, cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics (covering gut organisms) within an hour, and escalate to inotropes if shock persists after 40–60 mL/kg.

questions.question: A child with fever and a cold has a soft 2/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. He is well. What is the murmur?
questions.exp: Still's murmur: vibratory, musical, low-grade systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge in 3–6-year-olds, louder with fever, anaemia or exercise. It needs no investigation.

questions.question: An unvaccinated boy has fever, a swollen neck, a sore throat and a grey membrane on the tonsils. What is the organism?
questions.exp: Diphtheria: adherent grey pseudomembrane, "bull neck", risk of airway obstruction, myocarditis and neuropathy from the toxin. Give antitoxin plus penicillin or erythromycin, isolate, and treat and vaccinate contacts.

questions.question: A 12-year-old has fever, headache, sweating and body aches with a raised white cell count. What should be asked about in the history?
questions.a: Travel to a dengue area only
questions.exp: Brucellosis (from unpasteurised dairy products or contact with goats, sheep, cows and camels) is common in the Gulf: fever (often undulant), sweats, arthralgia, back pain, headache and hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.question: A fully vaccinated 7-year-old has had fever, sore throat and poor oral intake for 4 days and now has a new torticollis. He looks ill but not toxic. What is the treatment?
questions.b: IV antibiotics, with surgical drainage if there is no response (retropharyngeal abscess)
questions.exp: Fever, sore throat, neck stiffness or torticollis, drooling or dysphagia suggest a retropharyngeal abscess (mostly under 5 years, but older children too). Confirm with a contrast CT of the neck; treat with IV antibiotics (such as ampicillin–sulbactam or clindamycin), and drain if large or not responding.

questions.question: A girl with tachycardia is treated, and the new ECG shows a short PR interval and delta waves. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pre-excitation on the resting ECG after an SVT episode means an accessory pathway (WPW). Refer to cardiology; ablation is curative for recurrent episodes.

questions.question: An infant of a diabetic mother develops jitteriness and a murmur. What is the most likely cardiac diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fetal hyperinsulinism causes septal hypertrophy in infants of diabetic mothers, sometimes with left ventricular outflow obstruction. It resolves over months. Avoid inotropes; beta-blockers can help if obstructed. Jitteriness may also be from hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia or polycythaemia.

questions.question: In the labour room, a newborn has a heart rate of 70/min and a respiratory rate of 44 with poor effort. What is the treatment?
questions.d: Positive pressure ventilation with bag and mask
questions.exp: A heart rate below 100 after initial steps needs effective ventilation; most babies respond. Compressions start only if the heart rate stays below 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

questions.question: A 16-year-old hit his chest on the steering wheel in a car crash. He has breathlessness, chest pain, capillary refill of 3–4 seconds and hypotension. The chest X-ray shows no pneumothorax or haemothorax. What is the first step?
questions.c: A 20 mL/kg crystalloid or blood bolus, then reassess and look for the source of bleeding
questions.exp: Hypotension after trauma is haemorrhage until proven otherwise: give oxygen, two large IV lines, warmed fluid or blood boluses (in major trauma, early blood products in a 1:1 ratio), and search for bleeding (abdomen, pelvis, chest). Consider cardiac contusion or tamponade (muffled sounds, raised JVP).

questions.question: A 5-year-old who was 10% dehydrated with sodium 168 mmol/L was given 20 mL/kg saline, then maintenance fluids. Four hours later he deteriorates and becomes drowsy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.a: Cerebral oedema from too-rapid correction of sodium
questions.exp: In hypernatraemic dehydration, brain cells have adapted to the high osmolality; lowering sodium too fast draws water into them, causing cerebral oedema and seizures. Lower sodium by no more than 0.5 mmol/L per hour (10–12 mmol/L per day), rehydrating over 48–72 hours. Myelinolysis follows rapid correction of HYPOnatraemia.

questions.question: A 4 kg infant refuses feeds and is irritable, with a heart rate of 230/min, SVT on the ECG and weak peripheral pulses. What is the treatment?
questions.c: Synchronised DC cardioversion at 4 J (1 J/kg)
questions.exp: SVT with signs of shock (weak pulses, poor perfusion) needs synchronised cardioversion at 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg; IV adenosine can be tried first only if access is already in place without delay. Verapamil is contraindicated in infants.

questions.question: A child rescued from a house fire has a metabolic acidosis with a base deficit of 8. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Smoke inhalation causes tissue hypoxia from carboxyhaemoglobin and cyanide, giving lactic acidosis. Give 100% oxygen, measure COHb, and consider hydroxocobalamin for cyanide.

questions.question: A ventilated neonate with RDS suddenly deteriorates, and the chest X-ray shows a tension pneumothorax. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.a: Needle aspiration of the chest, followed by a chest drain
questions.exp: A tension pneumothorax (sudden desaturation, bradycardia, unequal chest movement, shift of the heart) needs needle decompression (2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, or 4th–5th space anterior axillary line) then a chest drain. Transillumination can help at the bedside.

questions.question: How often should transcranial Doppler screening be done in a child with sickle cell anaemia?
questions.c: Only if he has a stroke
questions.exp: TCD screening yearly from 2 to 16 years (more often if borderline) identifies children at high stroke risk (velocity over 200 cm/s), who then start regular transfusions.

questions.question: A child with ADHD has been doing well on treatment, but his school performance drops after he changes school. The dose is unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
questions.d: The drug has stopped working permanently
questions.exp: Transitions (new school, teachers, friends, more demands) commonly unsettle children with ADHD. Review the support plan with the new school, look for anxiety, bullying or mood problems, and check adherence before changing medication.

questions.question: A 1-year-old is exclusively breastfed by a vegan mother. He is pale with an MCV of 116 fL. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Breastfed infants of vegan mothers who do not take B12 supplements can develop B12 deficiency: macrocytic anaemia, faltering growth, hypotonia, developmental regression and irritability. Treat the baby (IM hydroxocobalamin) and the mother, and supplement during breastfeeding.

questions.question: A mother is worried about her 15-month-old's development. He says 5–15 words but no sentences, points to body parts and follows a single command without gestures. What should she be told?
questions.exp: At 15 months, children say several words (often 3–10), follow simple commands and point to show interest; two-word phrases come at about 2 years. This child is ahead in some areas, so reassure. Red flags: no words by 18 months, no pointing by 12–15 months, loss of skills.

questions.question: A 5-month-old has jerky movements with flexion of the head and limbs, mainly in the morning on waking. What is the expected EEG change?
questions.exp: Infantile spasms (West syndrome) occur in clusters, often on waking, with flexor or extensor spasms and developmental regression. The EEG shows hypsarrhythmia (chaotic high-voltage slow waves and multifocal spikes). 3 Hz spike-and-wave is absence epilepsy; centrotemporal spikes are self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes.

questions.question: A child with diabetic ketoacidosis (low pH, positive ketones) is improving. Which statement is true?
questions.b: Give insulin by IV bolus first
questions.c: Stop insulin as soon as glucose is normal
questions.d: Continue the insulin infusion until ketosis resolves, adding dextrose as glucose falls
questions.exp: In DKA, insulin (0.05–0.1 units/kg/hour) is needed to switch off ketogenesis; when glucose falls below about 14 mmol/L add dextrose to the fluids rather than stopping insulin, until pH and ketones normalise and the child can eat. Avoid insulin boluses and bicarbonate; give fluids cautiously because of cerebral oedema risk.

questions.question: Under Oman's Child Law, what right does every child have?
questions.a: Children have no right to be heard
questions.b: Children's rights apply only to citizens
questions.c: Non-discrimination on the basis of sex, race, religion or other status
questions.d: Parents can refuse all care with no limit
questions.e: Only boys have a right to education
questions.exp: Oman's Child Law (Royal Decree 22/2014), in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, protects children's rights to life, health care, education, protection from abuse and neglect, and equal treatment without discrimination by sex, origin, colour, disability or religion.

questions.question: A child with ADHD started a new treatment for depression 2 weeks ago and now has a dry mouth and drowsiness. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Tricyclics have anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision) and sedating antihistaminic effects, and they are dangerous in overdose. SSRIs are preferred for depression in young people.

questions.question: A child has a dry mouth, flushed skin and dilated pupils after taking a cough and cold remedy. Which drug is the likely cause?
questions.exp: First-generation antihistamines (pheniramine, chlorphenamine, diphenhydramine) have anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, flushing, mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention, agitation or drowsiness and seizures in overdose. Cough and cold medicines are not recommended for young children.

questions.question: What is the main effect of hydroxyurea in sickle cell disease?
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea raises HbF, reducing sickling, painful crises, acute chest syndrome and transfusion needs. Monitor blood counts.

questions.question: A neonate is pale and tachycardic with a haemoglobin of 4 g/dL and reticulocytes of 20%. Mother and baby are both O positive. What is the management?
questions.c: Urgent packed red cell transfusion, with a Kleihauer test and haematology review
questions.exp: Severe anaemia with a high reticulocyte count and no blood group incompatibility suggests chronic fetomaternal haemorrhage (Kleihauer test on the mother) or another haemolytic cause (G6PD, spherocytosis). A tachycardic baby with Hb 4 needs slow transfusion of packed cells (or partial exchange if in heart failure).

questions.question: An obese teenage girl has a limp without trauma. Hip abduction and internal rotation are restricted. What is the next step?
questions.e: Hip X-rays, including a frog-leg lateral view
questions.exp: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis: obese adolescents with hip, thigh or knee pain, limp, and loss of internal rotation (the leg turns out on flexion). AP and frog-leg lateral X-rays confirm. Stop weight bearing and arrange urgent orthopaedic pinning; check the other hip.

questions.question: A 10-month-old has had hypoglycaemia attacks since 3 months of age, with hepatomegaly, high lactate and high triglycerides. What is the diagnosis?
questions.a: Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke)
questions.exp: GSD I (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency): fasting hypoglycaemia from early infancy, large liver, doll-like face, lactic acidosis, hypertriglyceridaemia, hyperuricaemia and short stature; type Ib also has neutropenia. Frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch; avoid fructose and galactose.

questions.question: A boy has frequent falls and calf hypertrophy. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.e: Genetic testing for a dystrophin gene deletion or duplication
questions.exp: In suspected Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a very high CK is followed by dystrophin gene analysis (deletions or duplications in most, then sequencing), which has replaced muscle biopsy. Genetic counselling for the family (carrier mothers).

questions.question: An infant of a poorly controlled diabetic mother has a congenital anomaly that is particularly specific to maternal diabetes. What is it?
questions.exp: Infants of diabetic mothers have more congenital anomalies (linked to high HbA1c in early pregnancy): heart defects (TGA, VSD), neural tube defects, small left colon, renal anomalies, and caudal regression syndrome, which is rare but most strongly associated.

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl is short, but her growth velocity is normal and her bone age is 2 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A normal growth velocity with a delayed bone age suggests constitutional delay. GH deficiency also delays bone age, but the growth velocity is low. Familial short stature has a bone age equal to chronological age. Still check a karyotype in short girls if growth falters.

questions.question: A 3-year-old is brought in with an area of hair loss on the scalp, petechiae and a tender swelling 1.5 cm across. What should be done?
questions.b: Discharge with a review in a month
questions.e: CT head and referral to the child protection team
questions.exp: Traumatic alopecia with petechiae and a tender boggy swelling suggests forceful hair pulling causing a subgaleal haematoma, a sign of physical abuse. Assess for intracranial injury (CT), examine fully, do bloods for clotting, and refer to child protection.

questions.question: A mother is O positive and her baby is A positive, with a positive direct antiglobulin test. What will the blood film show?
questions.exp: ABO haemolytic disease: maternal anti-A IgG coats the baby's red cells, which are partly removed by the spleen, forming spherocytes; the marrow responds with reticulocytosis (polychromasia). Jaundice appears in the first 24 hours. Treat with phototherapy, and exchange or IVIG if severe.

questions.question: A child is investigated for bowed legs. His mother had rickets. ALP is high, phosphate is low and calcium is normal. Which investigation confirms renal phosphate wasting?
questions.a: Renal tubular phosphate threshold (TmP/GFR), with a normal or low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
questions.exp: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets: low TmP/GFR (renal phosphate wasting) from high FGF23, with an inappropriately normal or low 1,25-vitamin D, normal calcium and PTH. Treat with burosumab or phosphate plus calcitriol.

questions.question: A first-time mother has painful, cracked nipples when breastfeeding. What is the most likely cause?
questions.b: Poor latching (and positioning) of the baby
questions.exp: Sore, cracked nipples in the first weeks are mostly from a shallow latch. The baby should face the breast, nose to nipple, with a wide-open mouth taking much of the areola, the chin touching the breast and the lower lip turned out. Look for tongue-tie and thrush if pain continues.

questions.question: A child with severe allergic asthma is not controlled on high-dose inhaled steroid and oral prednisolone. Total IgE is 2000. Which add-on treatment fits?
questions.exp: Severe allergic asthma (GINA step 5) with raised IgE and sensitisation to a perennial allergen can be treated with omalizumab (anti-IgE); anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab) or anti-IL-4R (dupilumab) for eosinophilic asthma. Check adherence and technique first.

questions.question: What type of hypersensitivity reaction is anaphylaxis?
questions.exp: Type I: allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and other mediators within minutes. Serum tryptase is raised 1–3 hours after a reaction. Type IV is contact dermatitis or the tuberculin test.
